findings.what: 'So on this grid P⁻¹MP = [3 0; 0 2]' skips the step that makes it follow: in her numbers b₁ is (1, 0) and M takes it to 3b₁, which is (3, 0), and b₂ is (0, 1) and goes to 2b₂, which is (0, 2), so those are the columns, just as Matrices lesson 2's columns are where i and j land. Add that bridge and keep the screen near 90 words, for example by cutting 'Your j is knocked off its line, to (1, 2)', since the picture already shows j leaving its line.

findings.where: Screen 9, A move in her numbers (SHOW text)
findings.what: On the one screen about a quarter turn, 'turns' means two things side by side: 'P turns it into your (3, 3). M turns that to (−3, 3)' makes P read as a rotation. Give P and P⁻¹ another verb, such as 'rewrites' or 'brings back'. Replace 'Jennifer wants it in hers' with the goal itself: one matrix that takes her numbers in and gives her numbers out.

findings.where: Screen 4, What changed? (task and right answer)
findings.what: The right answer, 'Only the numbers', is not quite true, because the question itself says b₁ moved and her grid swung with it. Ask what changed for the arrow to (3, 3), or word the answer as 'Her numbers for it, not the arrow'.

findings.where: Whole lesson (where it is used, and what comes next)
findings.what: No screen links the idea to his trade or says where it goes next. The brief promised the Clarke transform here as a named change of basis that is shown but not worked: three phase quantities become two components at right angles (brief notes 4.8, not yet in research.json). The tray analogy appears only in the dossier, and screen 11 never says that lesson 6 is where such grids are found. One sourced sentence on screen 11 would fix all three.

findings.where: Lead above the stepper and caption below the frame (all 13 screens)
findings.what: The lead ('Her arrows are b₁ = (2, 1) and b₂ = (−1, 1)…') and the caption ('…P's columns are b₁ and b₂') stay on all 13 screens. They describe the wrong grid on screens 6, 11, 12 and 13. The caption also puts about 17 more words under every picture, though Dan asked for less text after the diagrams. Drop the caption, and make the lead neutral or set it per screen.

findings.where: Screens 11, 12 and 13 (names in the key, card and tasks)
findings.what: 'Her' means Jennifer's grid of (2, 1) and (−1, 1), but it is also used for three other grids. On screen 11 the key says 'her grid' and the card says 'M only stretches her arrows'. Screen 12 says 'Her grid is (1, 1) and (1, −1)', and screen 13 says 'Her arrows are (2, 1) and (4, 2)'. Call each of these 'a new grid', as screen 6's key already does.

findings.where: Screen 1, One arrow, two grids (text and picture)
findings.what: Jennifer appears with no word on who she is or why her grid differs. One clause, such as 'Suppose Jennifer measures with her own two arrows', fixes that. The first sentence also names i and j, which the picture never draws or labels.

findings.where: Screens 1, 3, 5 and 7 (the line under the picture, and the How button)
findings.what: 'How lays her amounts again, nose to tail.' uses the button's bare name as its subject and reads as broken English. Write 'The How button lays her amounts again, nose to tail', or rename the button 'Show how'.

findings.where: Screen 1 picture at 360 px (labels b₁ and b₂)
findings.what: The b₂ label sits on the dashed drag ring at b₂'s tip, and the b₁ label touches its ring, because label placement ignores the grips. Keep the labels clear of the 20 px rings.
'So P⁻¹ takes (4, 2) to (3, 1)' skips the working that screen 7 and screen 8's Why? both show. Add one line: [−1 −1; −1 1] times (4, 2) is (−6, −2), and ÷ (−2) gives (3, 1).

findings.where: Screen 2, Her numbers to yours (wrong answer (4, 1): hint and red line)
findings.what: The hint and the red line say only that (4, 1) 'mixes up the across and up parts', which does not show Dan what he did. Name the slip plainly, or show that 1 lot of b₁ plus 2 of b₂ lands on (0, 3), not (4, 1), as the other wrong answers do.
'The area is not 0, so P has an inverse' comes last, after P⁻¹ has already been worked out. Move it to just after the area sentence, so the reason comes before the working.
'Which product does the quarter turn in her numbers?' can be misread with 'does' as a question word. Write 'Which product gives the quarter turn in her numbers?'
[^2] sits on 'the same arrow usually gets different numbers', which is not a rule or value he would look up. Drop it and keep the footnote on the column rule.
